newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Chamber of Commerce slams regulation proposal.
newsitem.headline: HK Chamber of Commerce slams regulation proposal.

text.p: Hong Kong's General Chamber of Commerce lashed out on Wednesday at proposals by the territory's consumer affairs watchdog to impose commercial competition rules on the free-wheeling business sector.

"Implementation of the Consumer Council's proposals will mean a material increase in the regulation, control and intervention by government in the economic and business life of Hong Kong," chamber director Ian Christie said in a statement.

The Consumer Council issued a report last October arguing for the introduction of a comprehensive competition policy, enactment of a competition law and creation of an authority to oversee competition in the economy.
The council suggested giving the new authority the power to impose penalties for anti-competitive activities.
It should also be empowered to order companies to pay compensation in the case of uncompetitive business practices, to handle complaints and initiate investigations, the council said.
However, the British-ruled territory has prospered under minimal government intervention, and its business community is on guard against any assault on the laissez-faire system.

In a detailed, point-by-point rebuttal, the chamber said the council's proposals, if implemented, would mean a significant departure from the free-wheeling, non-interventionist policies for which Hong Kong has long been renowned.
"The Consumer Council's report proposes regulated trade and managed competition. It proceeds on the basis of a perception the market in Hong Kong is working badly," the chamber said.

"In reality, and judged by Hong Kong's economic performance, the market works well. This is illustrated by the 1996 report of the World Economic Forum, which ranked Hong Kong as the third most competitive economy in the world," it said.
The chamber also criticised the council for not furnishing enough evidence for its charge that there were sectors in which a lack of competition had forced up prices, fuelling inflation.
